question: How many total links make up the standard chain of infection?
explanation: The chain of infection consists of six distinct links that must all be present for an infection to spread. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h1)

question: What happens if a nurse successfully breaks just one link in the chain of infection?

options.A: The entire spread of infection stops
options.B: The susceptible host becomes instantly immune to all diseases
options.C: The causative agent changes into a harmless bacteria
options.D: The pathogen becomes stronger and multiplies faster

explanation: You've got this! Breaking any single link stops the pathogen from reaching a new host, successfully halting the infection cycle. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h1)

question: What do we call the natural home where a germ likes to live and multiply?
explanation: Think of a reservoir as the germ's cozy home base where it survives, grows, and multiplies before trying to move on. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why can non-living things like hospital bedrails act as hiding places for germs?

options.A: They maintain a constant body temperature for parasites
options.B: They provide a surface where pathogens can survive and multiply
options.C: They actively manufacture new viruses using room oxygen
options.D: They digest bacteria to make them more dangerous

explanation: Germs can linger on inanimate objects (called fomites) and use them as temporary resting spots until a hand or touch picks them up. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h2)

question: When someone coughs or sneezes, what part of the infection chain are they showing?
explanation: Coughing and sneezing expel respiratory secretions into the air, acting as a main exit door for the germs to leave the body. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the main difference between droplet spread and airborne spread?

options.A: Airborne transmission requires direct skin-to-skin contact
options.B: Airborne transmission only happens through contaminated water sources
options.C: Droplet particles are larger and travel only short distances
options.D: Droplet pathogens can only survive inside insect vectors

explanation: Heavy droplets quickly drop to the ground within a short range, whereas tiny airborne particles stay floating in the air much longer. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which medical device creates an artificial pathway for bacteria to enter the bladder?
explanation: Catheters bypass the body's natural protective barriers in the urethra, giving bacteria a direct highway straight into the bladder. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why is an elderly patient in the hospital usually a more susceptible host than a healthy adult?

options.A: Their immune system is naturally weaker and less responsive
options.B: Their body temperature is always too high for bacteria
options.C: Their skin is thicker and stops pathogens more effectively
options.D: Their blood circulation moves pathogens out too quickly

explanation: As we age or face illness, our immune system slows down, making it harder to fight off invading germs. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which nursing action directly stops germs from spreading from one patient to another?

options.A: Checking the patient's temperature every four hours
options.B: Performing hand hygiene and changing gloves between patients
options.C: Administering prescribed antibiotic therapy on schedule
options.D: Serving high-protein meals to improve overall nutrition

explanation: Washing your hands and changing gloves is your absolute best defense against carrying germs between patients! [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which nursing intervention is specially designed to destroy the causative agent itself?

options.A: Sterilizing surgical instruments in an autoclave
options.B: Applying lotion to dry, cracked skin
options.C: Isolating a patient in a private room
options.D: Educating patients on proper cough etiquette

explanation: Autoclaving uses high heat and pressure to wipe out microorganisms completely, destroying the causative agent before it touches a patient. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h5)
